anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model, indexes, partitions, constraints, and data types are mismatched to workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer decisions.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage media or controller cannot deliver the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required by the database, so physical I/O becomes the dominant wait state.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network links, listener processes, or connection-handling resources become saturated or unstable, delaying connection establishment and result transfer between clients and the database server.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, performance symptoms appear at every layer. Queries already forced into full-table scans or non-covering index lookups generate excess physical I/O that clashes with an undersized or congested storage subsystem, driving up disk queue depths and read/write latencies. The prolonged execution times keep server back-end sessions busy longer, inflating the active connection count just as network sockets, listener backlogs, or authentication threads are themselves bottlenecked. Clients observe timeouts both when establishing sessions and while waiting for large result sets; meanwhile the database shows a mixture of storage waits (data-file, log flush, temp I/O) and client/network waits (socket send/receive, TCP retransmits). CPU may appear under-utilised because time is consumed in I/O and network waits, masking the underlying schema inefficiencies.

Causally, poor schema and index design increases the volume and randomness of I/O. On an already throughput-limited storage layer this magnifies latency, which in turn prolongs transactions and amplifies concurrent session counts. The bloated execution windows and larger result sets place sustained pressure on network pipelines and connection pools, making network saturation and socket exhaustion more likely. Conversely, intermittent network slow-downs extend the life of each database session, reducing buffer cache turnover and forcing more dirty pages to accumulate and flush under constrained storage bandwidth, worsening I/O stalls. This feedback loop leads to cascading slowdowns: design flaws create excessive I/O, storage limits throttle throughput, and network/resource contention further extends query lifetimes—jointly degrading both transactional and analytical workload performance.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
